The installer offered the application path: “On any browser you can install firmware with the application instead,” followed by the link “Get Arranger and install it from there.” Its href was directly verified as /downloads.
The /doctor interactive-element inventory contained the application-path link but no Connect button or other camera connection control.
Following the offered path opened /downloads, where the page displayed “Download Arranger 2.0.0,” confirming the in-application alternative is available rather than a dead-end or empty page.
verdicts.rationale: In this browser lacking the required USB device capability, the firmware installer replaces connection controls with a complete explanation, explicitly names Chrome, Edge, and Opera on desktop as working browsers, and provides a functioning in-app route to obtain Arranger. No unusable connect control is rendered.

evidence: With one Travel Case in the cart and before entering a delivery address, the cart Summary directly displayed: “Estimated subtotal $79.00,” “Estimated delivery —,” “Estimated tax $7.90,” and “Estimated total $86.90.”
Directly below those estimated totals, the cart displayed the sentence: “Estimated. We will show the exact amount once we know where it is going.”
Submitting the blank address form produced inline required-field validation while the order summary continued to use the estimated labels and exact-amount-after-address sentence.

After entering reversible fixture address data and progressing through delivery selection to Payment, the review summary changed to unqualified figures: “Subtotal,” “Delivery (Standard),” “Tax,” and “Total,” confirming the estimate treatment applies before the delivery details are established.
verdicts.rationale: The pre-address cart explicitly labels delivery and tax as estimates and places an explanatory sentence immediately after the totals saying the exact amount will be shown once the destination is known. The completed flow also confirms those labels become final-style labels only after address and delivery information are supplied.

evidence: style criterion has no objective selector
On `/`, measured visible navigation/link styles were monochrome: `rgb(245, 243, 239)` text on either `rgb(30, 33, 41)` or transparent backgrounds.

On `/shop`, measured representative cart/navigation/product elements used neutral colors only: `rgb(26, 29, 35)`, `rgb(84, 89, 99)`, `rgb(146, 154, 170)`, and `rgb(240, 238, 235)`, with no saturated accent identified.
On `/shop/flagship`, the three finish tabs and radio inputs measured black/neutral styling; the Add to cart button was light text `rgb(249, 248, 246)` on a dark neutral `rgb(26, 29, 35)` background.

Screenshots were captured for `/`, `/shop`, and `/shop/flagship`, but this tool transport omitted the image content, so visual accent instances and bounding boxes could not be independently inspected.
verdicts.rationale: The measured routes provide evidence of a monochrome treatment and no detected saturated accent, but the criterion applies across shop, cart, account, and letter screens. Cart and account screens were not directly examined, and the screenshot content was unavailable for visual counting. Therefore the observations do not defensibly settle whether an accent appears at most once on every applicable screen.

evidence: Deterministic motion inventory on `/` found the only declared transitions at 0.12s with linear timing (transform and opacity), with reduced motion not active.

On authenticated `/shop`, computed styles for Cart, Shop, Orders, and Sign out controls consistently used 0.12s linear transitions; the Shop and account navigation controls used 0.12s linear for both background-color and color, while Cart used 0.12s linear opacity.
A direct CDP capture started immediately before a keyboard focus change recorded one transform transition with duration 120ms, easing `linear`, one iteration, and no delay.

On `/shop/flagship`, quantity and Add to cart controls both used 0.12s linear opacity transitions. The finish disclosure/tab switch produced no animation, changing immediately rather than introducing a different eased or spring motion.
No inspected control exposed spring-like easing, overshoot, bounce, or differing nonzero transition durations.
verdicts.rationale: Across the sampled shop, cart navigation, and authenticated account controls, every animated interaction uses the same short 120ms linear timing. Immediate state/disclosure changes do not introduce competing motion, and direct CDP capture corroborates the declared timing with no spring or overshoot.

evidence: At 1440×900 on /shop, the persistent navigation appeared as a 231px-wide left rail: the active Shop link occupied x=0–231 while shop content began at x=269.

After resizing /shop to 390×844 and refreshing references, the rail links were replaced by one button labeled “☰ Sections” spanning x=0–390 at y=80–129, above shop content; opening it revealed the former Browse, account, and session links.
At 390×844 on /cart, the same single “☰ Sections” control appeared at x=0–390, y=80–129 above the cart content, and expanded to reveal the rail links.
At 390×844 on /account, the navigation likewise appeared as the single “☰ Sections” button above account content.

After resizing /account back to 1440×900 and refreshing references, the button was absent and the persistent rail returned, with rail links occupying x=0–231 (for example Shop at y=122–159 and Overview at y=283–320).
verdicts.rationale: Direct responsive geometry and interaction checks establish the required transformation on all three specified areas: shop, cart, and account use a persistent left rail at wide width, collapse it to one top-of-content Sections control at phone width, and restore the rail when widened.

evidence: On route `/`, the interactive-elements snapshot lists three links: `Skip to the letter`, the `vela` wordmark, and `Shop`.

The `Shop` link is at y=3918 near the page footer and the page text ends with the footer row `vela / All rights reserved / Shop / Support / Terms / Privacy / Jobs / Contact`, so it is a footer element rather than an extra in-letter control.
The `Skip to the letter` anchor has `href="#letter"`, making it an in-page navigation element separate from the wordmark and footer.

After pressing Tab from the top of the page, `Skip to the letter` received keyboard focus and was visibly exposed at box (20,8) with a solid 2px focus outline, directly confirming that the extra navigation element is shown during interaction.
No price or form field was present on the letter route, but the extra skip-navigation link alone meets the criterion's OR condition.
verdicts.rationale: The letter includes a focus-revealed in-page navigation link, `Skip to the letter`, in addition to its wordmark and footer row. Because the rule says any navigation element beyond the wordmark/footer is sufficient, the negative anti-pattern is observed.
